claim: Human sex chromosomes are strongly heteromorphic, exhibiting extensive differences in size, gene number, DNA repeat abundance and heterochromatin composition.
source: The human sex chromosomes are strongly heteromorphic as they exhibit extensive differences in size, gene number, DNA repeat abundance and heterochromatin composition (Skaletsky et al., 2003; Ross et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Skaletsky et al., 2003 and Ross et al., 2005

claim: The human X chromosome comprises a large X-specific region recombining only in females.
source: The X chromosome comprises a large X-specific region recombining only in females whereas the Y comprises a male-specific region that does not recombine at all.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about human sex chromosomes

claim: The human Y chromosome comprises a male-specific region that does not recombine at all.
source: The X chromosome comprises a large X-specific region recombining only in females whereas the Y comprises a male-specific region that does not recombine at all.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about human sex chromosomes

claim: Both human sex chromosomes share two pseudoautosomal regions (PAR1 and 2) that recombine in both males and females.
source: Both sex chromosomes share two pseudoautosomal regions (PAR1 and 2) that recombine in both males and females.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about human sex chromosomes

claim: Human sex chromosomes originated from a pair of identical autosomes approximately 150 million years ago, prior to the divergence of placentals and marsupials.
source: These sex chromosomes originated from a pair of identical autosomes approximately 150 million years ago, prior to the divergence of placentals and marsupials, with the evolution of Sry – the master male-determining gene in therian mammals – from Sox3 (Lahn and Page, 1999; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Hughes and Rozen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahn and Page, 1999; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Hughes and Rozen, 2012

claim: The evolution of Sry from Sox3 occurred during the origin of human sex chromosomes.
source: These sex chromosomes originated from a pair of identical autosomes approximately 150 million years ago, prior to the divergence of placentals and marsupials, with the evolution of Sry – the master male-determining gene in therian mammals – from Sox3 (Lahn and Page, 1999; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Hughes and Rozen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahn and Page, 1999; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Hughes and Rozen, 2012

claim: Vast regions of the Y chromosome have stopped recombining with the X at several moments throughout evolutionary history, likely through inversions on the Y.
source: Since then, at several moments throughout evolutionary history, vast regions of the Y chromosome have stopped recombining with the X, likely through inversions on the Y (Lahn and Page, 1999; Van Laere et al., 2008; Lemaitre et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahn and Page, 1999; Van Laere et al., 2008; Lemaitre et al., 2009; Pandey et al., 2013

claim: Regions of the Y chromosome that stopped recombining show different levels of X-Y divergence and are called evolutionary strata.
source: These regions show different levels of X-Y divergence and are called evolutionary strata (Lahn and Page, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lahn and Page, 1999

claim: Strata 1 and 2 are shared among all therians.
source: Strata 1 and 2 are shared among all therians, and stratum three is shared among all placentals (Lahn and Page, 1999; Cortez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahn and Page, 1999; Cortez et al., 2014

claim: Stratum three is shared among all placentals.
source: Strata 1 and 2 are shared among all therians, and stratum three is shared among all placentals (Lahn and Page, 1999; Cortez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahn and Page, 1999; Cortez et al., 2014

claim: Strata 4 and 5 originated in the history of Catarrhini approximately 40 and 25 Mya, respectively.
source: The most recent strata (4 and 5) have originated in the history of Catarrhini (Old World monkeys and apes) respectively,~40 and~25 Mya, and now only a very small PAR continues to recombine between X and Y in those primates (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2012

claim: Only a very small PAR continues to recombine between X and Y in Catarrhini primates.
source: The most recent strata (4 and 5) have originated in the history of Catarrhini (Old World monkeys and apes) respectively,~40 and~25 Mya, and now only a very small PAR continues to recombine between X and Y in those primates (Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2012

claim: In humans, PAR1 is the consequence of recombination suppression, while PAR2 is a recent addition.
source: In humans, PAR1 is the consequence of that process, while PAR2 is a recent addition (Skaletsky et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skaletsky et al., 2003

claim: The process of recombination suppression between sex chromosomes, leading to a reduction in the size of the PAR and formation of evolutionary strata, has been documented in several animal and plant lineages.
source: The process of recombination suppression between sex chromosomes, leading to a reduction in the size of the PAR and formation of evolutionary strata, has been documented in several animal and plant lineages (e.g Nicolas et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2014; White et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicolas et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2014; White et al., 2015

claim: It has been proposed that sexually antagonistic mutations may have favoured the suppression of recombination.
source: It has been proposed that sexually antagonistic mutations may have favoured the suppression of recombination (Bull, 1983; Rice, 1987; Charlesworth et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bull, 1983; Rice, 1987; Charlesworth et al., 2005

claim: Theoretical models suggest that if there are male-beneficial/female-detrimental mutations in the PAR, there will be selection to halt recombination through for example an inversion to genetically link those mutations to the Y chromosome.
source: Theoretical models suggest that if there are male-beneficial/female-detrimental mutations in the PAR, there will be selection to halt recombination, through for example an inversion, to genetically link those mutations to the Y chromosome.
evidence: Based on theoretical models referenced in the context

claim: Some evidence supporting the sexually antagonistic mutations hypothesis has recently been found in guppies.
source: Some evidence supporting this hypothesis has recently been found in guppies (Wright et al., 2017), but evidence from a wide range of groups, including primates, is lacking.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2017

claim: Evidence from a wide range of groups, including primates, supporting the sexually antagonistic mutations hypothesis is lacking.
source: Some evidence supporting this hypothesis has recently been found in guppies (Wright et al., 2017), but evidence from a wide range of groups, including primates, is lacking.
evidence: Statement about the state of evidence in the field

claim: In strepsirrhines, female social dominance (FSD), in which females dominate males, is widespread and likely ancestral.
source: In strepsirrhines, female social dominance (FSD), in which females dominate males, is widespread and likely ancestral (Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015

claim: FSD in strepsirrhines is associated with increased testosterone production in females, resulting in the masculinization of females, including aspects of their social behaviour and genitalia.
source: FSD is associated with increased testosterone production in females, resulting in the masculinization of females, including aspects of their social behaviour and genitalia (Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015

claim: Some strepsirrhine species have rather egalitarian social systems.
source: Some species also have rather egalitarian social systems (Pereira and Kappeler, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pereira and Kappeler, 1997

claim: Sexual size dimorphism is virtually absent among strepsirrhines.
source: In addition, sexual size dimorphism is virtually absent among strepsirrhines (Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kappeler and Fichtel, 2015; Petty and Drea, 2015

claim: Sexual dimorphism is much more pronounced and male-biased in haplorrhines compared to strepsirrhines.
source: This is in sharp contrast with haplorrhines, where sexual dimorphism is much more pronounced and male-biased; a phenotype that is probably ancient in this group (e.g. Lindenfors, 2002; Kappeler and van Schaik, 2004; Plavcan, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindenfors, 2002; Kappeler and van Schaik, 2004; Plavcan, 2004

claim: Male-biased sexual dimorphism is probably ancient in haplorrhines.
source: This is in sharp contrast with haplorrhines, where sexual dimorphism is much more pronounced and male-biased; a phenotype that is probably ancient in this group (e.g. Lindenfors, 2002; Kappeler and van Schaik, 2004; Plavcan, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindenfors, 2002; Kappeler and van Schaik, 2004; Plavcan, 2004

claim: Strata 4 and 5 are missing in grey mouse lemurs (Microcebus murinus).
source: However, to date, very little is known about the sex chromosomes of strepsirrhines, except that strata 4 and 5 are missing in grey mouse lemurs (Microcebus murinus, see Glaser et al., 1999) preventing previous tests of this hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Glaser et al., 1999

claim: For autosomes, a M:F depth ratio of 1 is expected as males and females have the same copy number of autosomes.
source: For autosomes, a M:F depth ratio of 1 is expected as males and females have the same copy number of autosomes.
evidence: Based on established genetic principles

claim: On the X chromosome, a M:F depth ratio of 1 should indicate the PAR that is shared among sexes.
source: On the X chromosome, a ratio of 1 should indicate the PAR that is shared among sexes, a ratio of 0.5 should indicate the X-specific region as males have only one such region and females two, and the boundary between both would indicate the PAB.
evidence: Based on established genetic principles and methodology

claim: On the X chromosome, a M:F depth ratio of 0.5 should indicate the X-specific region as males have only one such region and females two.
source: On the X chromosome, a ratio of 1 should indicate the PAR that is shared among sexes, a ratio of 0.5 should indicate the X-specific region as males have only one such region and females two, and the boundary between both would indicate the PAB.
evidence: Based on established genetic principles and methodology

claim: The boundary between M:F depth ratios of 1 and 0.5 on the X chromosome indicates the PAB.
source: On the X chromosome, a ratio of 1 should indicate the PAR that is shared among sexes, a ratio of 0.5 should indicate the X-specific region as males have only one such region and females two, and the boundary between both would indicate the PAB.
evidence: Based on established genetic principles and methodology

claim: Seven species representing the main strepsirrhine lineages representing 65 My of evolution were studied.
source: Using Illumina short-read sequencing technology, we sequenced a male and a female genome in seven species covering the main strepsirrhine lineages representing 65 My of evolution (Pozzi et al., 2014): four Lemuriformes (Daubentonia madagascariensis - aye-ayes, M. murinus – grey mouse lemur, Eulemur rubriventer – red-bellied lemur, Prolemur simus – greater bamboo lemur) and three Lorisiformes (Otolemur garnettii – northern greater galago, Galago senegalensis – senegal bushbaby, Nyctibebus coucang – slow loris).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pozzi et al., 2014 for evolutionary time

claim: The sequencing depth of each sample was between 11.8X and 39.1X.
source: The sequencing depth of each sample was between 11.8X and 39.1X (assuming a genome size identical to the human genome) with 78% of the samples being between 20X and 40X, that is moderate sequencing depth (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Data from sequencing reported in Supplementary file 1A

claim: 78% of the samples had sequencing depth between 20X and 40X, representing moderate sequencing depth.
source: The sequencing depth of each sample was between 11.8X and 39.1X (assuming a genome size identical to the human genome) with 78% of the samples being between 20X and 40X, that is moderate sequencing depth (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Data from sequencing reported in Supplementary file 1A

claim: Using the human X chromosome to order the grey mouse lemur X scaffolds, the scaffolds corresponding to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 have a M:F depth ratio around 1.
source: Using the human X chromosome to order the grey mouse lemur X scaffolds, we found that the scaffolds corresponding to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 have a M:F depth ratio around 1 (Figure 1B), indicating that these regions have remained pseudoautosomal in grey mouse lemurs in agreement with older cytogenetic data (Glaser et al., 1999).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to Glaser et al., 1999

claim: The regions corresponding to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 have remained pseudoautosomal in grey mouse lemurs.
source: Using the human X chromosome to order the grey mouse lemur X scaffolds, we found that the scaffolds corresponding to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 have a M:F depth ratio around 1 (Figure 1B), indicating that these regions have remained pseudoautosomal in grey mouse lemurs in agreement with older cytogenetic data (Glaser et al., 1999).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to Glaser et al., 1999

claim: The rest of the grey mouse lemur X is X-specific with a M:F ratio close to 0.5.
source: The rest of the grey mouse lemur X is X-specific with a M:F ratio close to 0.5.
evidence: Data from the analysis

claim: Five regions in the X-specific region of grey mouse lemur show an elevated M:F depth ratio.
source: However, five regions in the X-specific region show an elevated ratio.
evidence: Data from the analysis

claim: Detailed analysis of the five regions with elevated M:F ratio in grey mouse lemur showed that they are fragments of autosomes.
source: Detailed analysis of these five regions showed that they are fragments of autosomes (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Data from detailed analysis reported in Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1B

claim: The regions homologous to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 are still recombining in grey mouse lemur.
source: Despite these limitations, it is nonetheless clear that the regions homologous to human PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 are still recombining in grey mouse lemur.
evidence: Inference from the M:F depth ratio data

claim: In all seven strepsirrhine species studied, the pattern of M:F depth ratio is very similar.
source: However, in all seven species studied here, the pattern is very similar (Figure 1C and a zoom on the PABs in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: All studied strepsirrhines harbour a large pseudoautosomal region including the genes that are in PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 in humans.
source: All studied strepsirrhines harbour a large pseudoautosomal region including the genes that are in PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 in humans (compare Figure 1A and C for lemurs and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and C for lorises; both lemur and loris PABs correspond to the boundary between human strata 4 and 3).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1A, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Both lemur and loris PABs correspond to the boundary between human strata 4 and 3.
source: All studied strepsirrhines harbour a large pseudoautosomal region including the genes that are in PAR1 and strata 4 and 5 in humans (compare Figure 1A and C for lemurs and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and C for lorises; both lemur and loris PABs correspond to the boundary between human strata 4 and 3).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1A, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: No suppression of recombination between the X and the Y has occurred in strepsirrhines since the origin of the group >65 millions years ago.
source: We can therefore conclude that no suppression of recombination between the X and the Y has occurred in strepsirrhines since the origin of the group >65 millions years ago (Figure 2).
evidence: Inference from the data shown in Figure 2 and previous analyses

claim: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be one for the PAR.
source: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be one for the PAR, <1 for old strata due to haploidy in males and >1 for recent strata due to accumulation of fixed X-Y differences (Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2017

claim: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be <1 for old strata due to haploidy in males.
source: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be one for the PAR, <1 for old strata due to haploidy in males and >1 for recent strata due to accumulation of fixed X-Y differences (Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2017

claim: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be >1 for recent strata due to accumulation of fixed X-Y differences.
source: The M:F SNP density ratio is predicted to be one for the PAR, <1 for old strata due to haploidy in males and >1 for recent strata due to accumulation of fixed X-Y differences (Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2017

claim: The analyses revealed no recent strata in the seven strepsirrhine species studied.
source: However, our analyses revealed no recent strata in the seven strepsirrhine species studied here (Figure 3).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 3

claim: In primates, two strata (4 and 5) were formed in apes and Old World monkeys.
source: However, the rate of strata formation is generally low: in primates two strata (4 and 5) were formed in apes and Old World monkeys, one was formed independently in New World monkeys (4') based on the species studied so far (Hughes et al., 2012; Cortez et al., 2014, and see Figure 2) and our additional data found no new strata formation in strepsirrhines.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hughes et al., 2012; Cortez et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 2

claim: One stratum was formed independently in New World monkeys (4').
source: However, the rate of strata formation is generally low: in primates two strata (4 and 5) were formed in apes and Old World monkeys, one was formed independently in New World monkeys (4') based on the species studied so far (Hughes et al., 2012; Cortez et al., 2014, and see Figure 2) and our additional data found no new strata formation in strepsirrhines.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hughes et al., 2012; Cortez et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 2

claim: No new strata formation was found in strepsirrhines.
source: However, the rate of strata formation is generally low: in primates two strata (4 and 5) were formed in apes and Old World monkeys, one was formed independently in New World monkeys (4') based on the species studied so far (Hughes et al., 2012; Cortez et al., 2014, and see Figure 2) and our additional data found no new strata formation in strepsirrhines.
evidence: Data from this study shown in Figure 2

claim: Comparing rates of strata formation on a time-based scale was only marginally significant (binomial test, p=0.051).
source: We designed a statistical test to compare the rates of strata formation (expressed in event per My) taking into account the respective divergence times in the haplorrhine and strepsirrhine parts of the phylogenetic tree of the studied species, but this test was only marginally significant (binomial test, p=0.051 see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical test performed on the data

claim: Rescaling time in generations to compare rates of strata formation lead to a significantly higher rate in haplorrhines (binomial test, p=0.01).
source: Rescaling time in generations to compare rates of strata formation (expressed in event per million generations) lead to a significantly higher rate in haplorrhines (binomial test, p=0.01 see Materials and methods), consistent with our hypothesis.
evidence: Statistical test performed on the data

claim: The sets of strepsirrhine and haplorrhine species differ significantly in sexual dimorphism (teeth and body size).
source: We collected phenotypic data from the literature for our set of 13 primate species and confirmed that our sets of strepsirrhine and haplorrhine species differ significantly in sexual dimorphism (teeth and body size, assuming that they reflect the global level of sexual dimorphism in an organism; see Materials and methods and Table 1) but not in sperm competition (testes size, see Materials and methods and Table 1).
evidence: Data collected from literature and analyzed, shown in Table 1

claim: The sets of strepsirrhine and haplorrhine species do not differ significantly in sperm competition (testes size).
source: We collected phenotypic data from the literature for our set of 13 primate species and confirmed that our sets of strepsirrhine and haplorrhine species differ significantly in sexual dimorphism (teeth and body size, assuming that they reflect the global level of sexual dimorphism in an organism; see Materials and methods and Table 1) but not in sperm competition (testes size, see Materials and methods and Table 1).
evidence: Data collected from literature and analyzed, shown in Table 1

claim: During primate evolution, the PAB has remained unchanged in strepsirrhines while several X-Y recombination suppression events have shortened the PAR in haplorrhines.
source: Our work shows that, during primate evolution, the PAB has remained unchanged in strepsirrhines while several X-Y recombination suppression events have shortened the PAR in haplorrhines.
evidence: Summary of the data from this study

claim: The difference in PAB evolution between strepsirrhines and haplorrhines is interpreted as a consequence of differences in sexual dimorphism, and therefore sexual conflict, in both groups.
source: We interpreted this as a consequence of differences in sexual dimorphism, and therefore sexual conflict, in both groups.
evidence: Interpretation of the data by the authors

claim: In guppies, populations exhibiting stronger sexual dimorphism seem to have a larger non-recombining region.
source: In guppies, while the Y chromosome exhibits low levels of divergence from the X (Wright et al., 2017; Bergero et al., 2019; Darolti et al., 2019), populations exhibiting stronger sexual dimorphism seem to have a larger non-recombining region (Wright et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2019; Almeida et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wright et al., 2017; Wright et al., 2019; Almeida et al., 2020

claim: In the brown alga Ectocarpus, sexual dimorphism is extremely low and sex chromosomes are homomorphic, with a small non-recombining region, despite being very old.
source: In the brown alga Ectocarpus, sexual dimorphism is extremely low and as expected sex chromosomes are homomorphic, with a small non-recombining region, despite being very old (Ahmed et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ahmed et al., 2014

claim: In ruminants, the PAR seems to have undergone a process of attrition due to accumulation of DNA repeats.
source: In ruminants, the PAR seems to have undergone a process of attrition due to accumulation of DNA repeats (Van Laere et al., 2008; Raudsepp and Chowdhary, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Laere et al., 2008; Raudsepp and Chowdhary, 2016

claim: In Microbotryum violaceum, strata are found on the mating-type chromosomes despite the fact that this species only has mating types and not sexes, such that sexual antagonism is absent.
source: In Microbotryum violaceum, strata are found on the mating-type chromosomes despite the fact that this species only has mating types and not sexes, such that sexual antagonism is absent (Branco et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Branco et al., 2017

claim: Sexually antagonistic mutation may not be a ubiquitous explanation of strata formation in all organisms.
source: Thus, sexually antagonistic mutation may not be a ubiquitous explanation of strata formation in all organisms.
evidence: Inference from the examples provided

claim: The genus Eulemur exhibits the most pronounced sexual dimorphism among strepsirrhines.
source: Although sexual dimorphism is generally low in strepsirrhines, there are some differences among species in this lineage, with the genus Eulemur exhibiting the most pronounced sexual dimorphism (Petty and Drea, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petty and Drea, 2015

claim: In Eulemur species, including the red-bellied lemur (E. rubriventer), males and females exhibit striking sexual dichromatism in pelage colouration.
source: In these species, including the red-bellied lemur (E. rubriventer), which was analysed here, males and females exhibit striking sexual dichromatism, that is they differ in pelage colouration (Rakotonirina et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rakotonirina et al., 2017

claim: The red-bellied lemur did not show more evidence for recombination suppression than the other strepsirrhine species studied.
source: The red-bellied lemur did not show more evidence for recombination suppression than the other species studied here.
evidence: Data from this study

claim: Sexual dichromatism antagonism might have been solved through sex-biased expression rather than Y-linkage.
source: Sexual dichromatism may rely on sexually antagonistic mutations. The antagonism might have been solved not through Y-linkage but instead through sex-biased expression for example (Ellegren and Parsch, 2007; Gazda et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Ellegren and Parsch, 2007; Gazda et al., 2020

claim: The haplorrhine lineages in the sample have evolved for 188.52 My (44.23 million generations) during which 3 new strata were formed.
source: The haplorrhine lineages in our sample have evolved for Δt1 = 188.52 My (44.23 million generations) during which S1 = 3 new strata were formed.
evidence: Data from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The strepsirrhine lineages evolved for 321.32 My (158.52 million generations) and no new strata was formed.
source: The strepsirrhine lineages evolved for Δt2 = 321.32 My (158.52 million generations) and no new strata was formed (S2 = 0).
evidence: Data from phylogenetic analysis

claim: Sexual dimorphism based on body mass (SSD) was 0.378 ± 0.097 in haplorrhines and 0.062 ± 0.017 in strepsirrhines.
source: Sexual dimorphism based on body mass (SSD, mean ± standard error) was 0.378 ± 0.097 in haplorrhines and 0.062 ± 0.017 in strepsirrhines.
evidence: Data from statistical analysis

claim: The difference in body mass sexual dimorphism between haplorrhines and strepsirrhines was statistically significant only when ignoring phylogenetic inertia (p=0.043).
source: This difference based on n = 13 observations was statistically significant only when ignoring phylogenetic inertia (p=0.043) but no longer significant when considering phylogenetic inertia with a Brownian motion model (p=0.66).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the data

claim: Sexual dimorphism based on canine height (CSD) was 0.385 ± 0.076 in haplorrhines and 0.045 ± 0.016 in strepsirrhines.
source: Sexual dimorphism based on canine height (CSD) showed the same kind of pattern: the mean is 0.385 ± 0.076 in haplorrhines and 0.045 ± 0.016 in strepsirrhines.
evidence: Data from statistical analysis

claim: The difference in canine height sexual dimorphism between haplorrhines and strepsirrhines is only significant when ignoring the underlying phylogeny (p=0.013).
source: This difference based on n = 12 observations is only significant when ignoring the underlying phylogeny (p=0.013) but no longer significant (p=0.39) when phylogeny is accounted for with a Brownian motion model (leading to a non different from 0 estimate of Pagel's λ).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the data

claim: The average relative testes mass did not significantly differ between haplorrhines (0.18 ± 0.24) and strepsirrhines (−0.21 ± 0.32).
source: Based on our n = 11 observations, the average relative testes mass did not significantly differ between haplorrhines (0.18 ± 0.24) and strepsirrhines (−0.21 ± 0.32).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the data
